newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian-Chechen tension rises after bomb blast.
newsitem.headline: Russian-Chechen tension rises after bomb blast.

text.p: Tension between Russia and rebel Chechnya, already simmering over stalled peace talks, rose on Tuesday to its highest level since a ceasefire last August amid mutal recriminations over a fatal bomb attack.
Russian police also fought a brief night-time skirmish with a group of what they said were 20 Chechen fighters just outside Chechnya, inflicting casualties on both sides.

Russian Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov said police had detained two Chechen women fighters suspected of organising an explosion in the spa resort of Pyatigorsk on Monday which killed two people and wounded more than 20 at a railway station.

Kulikov, who is also a deputy prime minister, said the two were part of a Chechen armed group which attacked the Russian town of Budennovsk in 1995 and staged a bloody hostage drama in which more than 100 people were killed.
"These are not rebels. This is not a political struggle, this is banditry," Kulikov said. "We will catch and destroy those criminals."
The accusations were immediately denied by Chechen Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov, Itar-Tass news agency said.

The separatist leaders, who fought a nearly 21-month conflict with Russian troops that killed tens of thousands before last August's truce, accused unnamed Russian special services of planting the bomb to disrupt the peace process.

"The leadership of the Chechen republic protests to the Russian authorities over the groundless accusations that the Chechen side was involved in the explosions at the railway stations," Tass quoted a statement by Chechen presidential spokesman Kazbek Khadzhiyev as saying.
A bomb explosion at Armavir railway station in southern Russia last Wednesday also killed two people.
Kulikov said he feared Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov, a relative moderate elected in January, was losing control.

"It has become evident that there is no unity in the Chechen leadership and Maskhadov may be unable to control the situation," said Kulikov, who commanded Russia's forces in Chechnya until he became interior minister in July 1995.
"If Maskhadov does not get rid of terrorists in his entourage, his regime will become a criminal one," he added.

Kulikov added that the people of the north Caucasus had demanded that Moscow take harsh measures against Chechen "bandits" and said there was a danger of pogroms of Chechens in Russia after "terrorist acts" by Chechens.
"The situation in the north Caucasus is becoming extremely tense. I am afraid it could become uncontrollable, Chechen pogroms may start," he said.
Kulikov's remarks sounded similar to those which Moscow officials made late in 1994 on the eve of military intervention in Chechnya, which they called a haven for criminals.
President Boris Yeltsin, who has called the decision to use military force to quell Chechen separatists a mistake, was following the situation closely.
Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky told Tass the president was extremely concerned and wanted the law and order bodies to take the "most tough and resolute...actions".
The ceasefire signed last August halted fighting but did not resolve the main dispute -- whether the rebel region is part of Russia or independent.

They two sides are now involved in difficult negotiations over a lasting peace treaty intendedto open the way for Moscow's help in restoring Chechnya, much of which has been destroyed by Russian air and artillery attacks.
Chechen vice-president Vakha Arsanov, quoted by Interfax news agency, said talks on political matters were impossible until Kulikov apologised for his remarks or proved them.
Kulikov also said police had fought a gun battle for more than two hours with 20 fighters who tried to cross from separatist Chechnya into the southern region of Dagestan.
Reports that there had been deaths in the incident, one of the most serious clashes since the ceasefire, could not be confirmed independently.
